$comment: Canonical token-introspection conditions: what auth-service (the center) answers, and what a calling service must answer its own caller for each. Source of truth for the conformance tests in the TS introspection client package (fleet-service, automation-service, st-gateway), agent-service (Go) and navigation-service (Java), which vendor this file verbatim. See ../docs/design/token-introspection.md and auth-design.md decision 21. DECIDED 2026-09-20, NOT SHIPPED: no service behaves this way yet — rollout is meta#80. Assertion vocabulary: a case is a route declaration, an inbound Authorization header, a stubbed center, and the expected outcome. `route.requires` is "none" (no credential declared), "session" (any verified session) or a scope literal. `expect.outcome` is "proceed" (the middleware ran the handler) or "reject". `expect.identity` is the {sub, kind, scopes} handed to the handler, or null for a visitor. `expect.centerCalls` is how many HTTP requests the client made to the center for this one inbound request — 0 and 1 are both assertions, and 2 fails. An unknown key in `expect` must fail the case rather than be skipped, or a copy that falls behind quietly checks less. No case may be satisfiable by an empty or absent answer: every rejection asserts its exact message, every proceed asserts the identity, and every case asserts the call count (meta#79).

messages.missingScope: this action requires a scope this session does not carry
messages.centerUnavailable: the authentication service did not answer, so this request cannot be authorized

contract.$messagesComment: The first three are quoted from the verifiers live today in agent-service/src/api/auth.go, fleet-service/src/auth.ts, auth-service/src/api/auth.go and navigation-service ClerkAuthFilter.java, and must stay byte-identical — the family envelope and these exact sentences are why command-interface needs one parser for every backend's auth rejections, including navigation-service, which emits RFC 9457 everywhere else and makes a deliberate exception here. automation-service's 403 names the scope today; it converges on `missingScope` as it migrates. The fourth is new with decision 21.
contract.$tokenComment: A calling service never parses, decodes or validates the token. The strings below are deliberately not valid JWTs: a client that looks inside one, or rejects one for being unparseable, fails these cases by answering before the center is asked.

cases.name: visitor-on-public-get
cases.why: The anonymous read surface (auth-design.md decision 2). No credential was presented, so there is nothing to introspect and the center must not be touched — a client that calls it anyway puts a synchronous dependency in front of every public page load and takes the dashboard down with auth-service.

cases.name: operator-on-public-get
cases.why: A public GET that does carry a token: the center IS called, and the verified identity reaches the handler. navigation-service's live-fetch rule and automation-service's actor recording both depend on knowing who a caller is on a route that would have served them anonymously. A client that short-circuits every GET serves this request correctly and silently loses the identity.

cases.name: no-header-on-guarded-route
cases.why: The declared-scope case with nothing presented. 401 and the family's own sentence, and the center is never asked: an unauthenticated flood must not become a flood against the center.

cases.name: non-bearer-scheme-on-guarded-route
cases.why: `Authorization: Basic …` is not a bearer token and never becomes one. It reads as no credential at all — the same 401 and the same sentence as a missing header, matching every verifier live today — all five key on the scheme case-insensitively and discard anything else. A client that forwards the raw header value, or the base64 blob after the scheme, calls the center with something that is not a token and turns a 401 into a 503 the first time the center is slow.

cases.name: inactive-token-on-public-get
cases.why: The rule that matters most on a public route: a presented credential that does not verify is a 401 on every method, never a quiet downgrade to visitor. Downgrading would let an expired session read the public surface while hiding the fact that its token died, and would hide a misconfigured trust anchor in the center. navigation-service already states this as an invariant; decision 21 does not relax it.

cases.name: inactive-token-on-guarded-route
cases.why: The same verdict on a mutating route, stated separately because the two travel through different branches of a middleware that splits on method. The message is the invalid-session one, not the missing-token one: something was presented and it was bad.

cases.name: active-with-required-scope
cases.why: The ordinary authorized mutation. Asserts the identity reaches the handler, not merely that the request was allowed: automation-service writes detail.actor from it and a middleware that authorizes without publishing the identity passes a status-only assertion.

cases.name: active-without-required-scope
cases.why: 403 rather than 401 — the session is valid, so re-authenticating would only loop. The message is generic and must NOT name the scope the route wanted: naming it turns every guarded route into a directory of the permissions worth stealing. automation-service names it today (`this action requires the "fleet:control" scope`) and is the one that has to change.

expect.message: this action requires a scope this session does not carry

cases.name: active-with-multi-value-scope
cases.why: `scope` is one space-delimited string, returned verbatim by the center whether the Clerk claim was a string or an array. A client comparing the whole string to the required literal passes every single-scope case above and fails here — which is the operator's real token, carrying all three scopes.

cases.name: active-machine-kind
cases.why: automation-service's M2M token (decision 19). It authorizes exactly like an operator's session — the scopes are baked into the token — but the handler must be able to tell the two apart: automation-service's knob-class fence restricts a machine caller to `policy` knobs. The discriminator is `kind`, never the presence of a header, because after decision 21 every caller presents one. A client that drops `kind` opens the alert and model knobs to the AI supervisor's path.

cases.name: mutating-route-with-no-declared-scope
cases.why: Default-deny, and the whole structural point of decision 21. A non-GET route that declares nothing is rejected even for a token that would satisfy any scope asked of it — that is what makes another meta#71 (an unauthenticated POST nobody remembered to guard) impossible rather than merely unlikely. The center is NOT called: a route that can never be authorized has nothing to verify, and answering before the hop keeps a misdeclared route from becoming load on the center. Asserting 403 with the generic sentence also means a misconfiguration tells the caller nothing it could not already guess.

expect.message: this action requires a scope this session does not carry

cases.name: center-times-out
cases.why: The center answers, but after the 1 s client timeout. 503, one sentence, and exactly ONE call: a retry against a center that is down doubles the latency of every failing request and changes nothing. `centerCalls: 1` is the assertion that catches a helpful retry loop, which no status assertion would.

expect.message: the authentication service did not answer, so this request cannot be authorized

cases.name: center-unreachable
cases.why: No response at all — connection refused, DNS failure, or a socket that died mid-body. Fail-closed: the mutation does not proceed, and it is a 503 rather than a 401, because nothing was learned about the caller's token. automation-service's classifier maps this to `unavailable`, so an auth outage costs a tick and never a target's retry budget.

expect.message: the authentication service did not answer, so this request cannot be authorized

cases.name: center-returns-500
cases.why: The center is reachable and broken. Same answer as unreachable, deliberately: the caller's remedy is identical and the distinction is the center's own business, in the center's own logs. A client that relays 500 makes an auth outage look like a bug in the service the operator is actually calling.

expect.message: the authentication service did not answer, so this request cannot be authorized

cases.name: center-rejects-our-caller-secret
cases.why: The center answers 401 — about OUR introspection secret, not about the end user's token. It must surface as 503, never as 401. Relaying it would tell an operator their session had expired when in fact a stack was deployed without AUTH_INTROSPECTION_SECRET or with a rotated one, and they would sign in again, repeatedly, against a service that can never accept them. This is the single easiest case for a lazy client to get wrong, because relaying the upstream status is the habit `upstream-errors.md` teaches for a different upstream.

expect.message: the authentication service did not answer, so this request cannot be authorized

cases.name: center-returns-malformed-json
cases.why: A 200 whose body is not the contract — a proxy error page, a truncated write, a half-deployed center. Unparseable is not `active:false`: treating it as an inactive token turns an outage into a fleet-wide 401 storm and tells the operator their credential is broken when it is not.

expect.message: the authentication service did not answer, so this request cannot be authorized

cases.name: token-on-public-get-while-center-is-down
cases.why: The case that decides what fail-closed means for the public surface. A visitor with no header keeps reading (see `visitor-on-public-get`); a caller who DID present a token gets 503, not a silent downgrade to visitor. Downgrading would be a read served under an identity nobody verified, and — worse — an operator would see the anonymous view with no indication that anything was wrong.

expect.message: the authentication service did not answer, so this request cannot be authorized

$gatewayCasesComment: st-gateway ONLY. A different policy, in its own group so nothing copies it by accident: the gateway does not authorize anything (that happened once already, in the calling service), it picks a queue lane. It therefore NEVER rejects and never answers 503 — a gateway that failed closed on the center would take the public read surface down with auth-service, which is exactly what the cases above are written to avoid. Anything other than an active `operator` is `background`, including a center that does not answer. `expect.lane` is the only verdict; a case that produces a status code fails. st-gateway consumes these through the same TS client package as fleet-service and automation-service, so both groups must be driven by its suite.

gatewayCases.name: gateway-no-header
gatewayCases.why: auth-service's own wipe poll and any anonymous visitor's live read. No credential, no call to the center, background lane. A gateway that called the center on every anonymous request would put auth-service on the hot path of the public map.

gatewayCases.name: gateway-non-bearer-scheme
gatewayCases.why: Not a bearer token, so nothing to introspect. Background, and the center is not asked — the same scheme check as every other client, and the only case here that must not produce a call.

gatewayCases.name: gateway-active-operator
gatewayCases.why: The only path to `interactive`. The dashboard's responsiveness is this case: a human session forwarded verbatim by agent/fleet/navigation-service. Note that the lane is decided by `kind`, not by the gateway inspecting `sub` — after decision 21 the center is the one place Clerk's sub conventions are known.

gatewayCases.name: gateway-active-machine
gatewayCases.why: automation-service's M2M token: a perfectly valid, fully scoped session that must still queue behind the browser. A client that maps any active token to `interactive` lets the autopilot outrank the operator watching it.

gatewayCases.name: gateway-inactive-token
gatewayCases.why: An expired or foreign-signed token. Background, NOT a 401 — the gateway is not the place a bad credential is refused, and the calling service in front of it has already refused it if the route was guarded.

gatewayCases.name: gateway-center-unreachable
gatewayCases.why: The case that separates this group from every other. auth-service being down must not stop the gateway proxying: the fleet's own calls and the public read surface both keep working, in the background lane. If this case ever answers 503, an auth outage becomes a total outage.

gatewayCases.name: gateway-center-rejects-our-caller-secret
gatewayCases.why: A misconfigured or rotated introspection secret. Still a lane decision, still background — the gateway degrades the operator's latency and nothing else. The calling services answer 503 for the same center response; the difference is deliberate and is why this group exists.
